newsitem.title: USA: Fed on hold in 96, tightening in 97 -- Bankers Trust.
newsitem.headline: Fed on hold in 96, tightening in 97 -- Bankers Trust.

text.p: The Federal Reserve will likely keep monetary policy on hold in 1996 and then adopt a tightening mode that may push up short-term rates by 50 to 75 basis points in 1997, said a top Bankers Trust official.

"The Fed will not change policy this year ... But I believe we can expect a 50 to 75 basis-point hike (in the federal funds rate) next year," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
The central bank's federal funds target is currently set at 5-1/4 percent. The Fed last changed that target in January 1996, when it cut rates by 25 basis points.
Williams said the economy is running at full employment and any further job gains and extra economic growth could lead to inflationary pressures down the road.

"The economy is operating at full employment and the growth rate is running at the speed limit," Williams said. "Two percent (annual Gross Domestic Product) growth is still the speed limit for the U.S. economy," he added.
The Bankers Trust official also predicted a recent rally in the U.S. Treasury market, which brought long-term yields to the lowest levels in eight months, will not last much longer.

Williams sees the yield on the U.S. benchmark 30-year bond moving towards 7.0 percent by the end of the year and to around 7.50 percent by mid-1997. The yield on the T-bond is currently near 6.48 percent.
Williams said the rise in bond yields was likely to follow a pick up in the economy in the fourth quarter of 1996 as consumers resume spending ahead of the year-end holidays.
"The economy is going to re-accelarate in the fourth quarter ... consumers will come back. The consumer fundamentals are extremely strong," Williams said.
Bankers Trust manages more than $200 billion in assets for institutions and individuals around the world.
